The biggest issue with an AI "safety slowdown:"

What happens with China?

While there are legitimate concerns around the safety of AI and how quickly it is evolving, the AI race is global.

And, in today's ecosystem, falling even 6 months behind in the AI race is like falling decades behind in the pre-AI world.

If US AI giants agree to slow progress and focus on safety, there must be an international agreement in place as well.

And, even if there is an agreement in place, how do we regulate compliance?

We've said it before and we will say it again: AI is the biggest technological revolution in history.

This is an AI arms race that may be impossible to fully regulate.

a16z's David George says AI's power law is becoming more extreme because dollars alone can compound a company's advantage:

"Right now, clearly the power law is more extreme than it has been in the last 10 to 20 years of technology investing, probably going back to the emergence of the network effect-driven consumer companies."

"Increasing returns to scale have always been a dynamic in our business... Brand reputation in the market, the accumulation of resources, all provide competitive advantages."

"That all still is the case. But right now, especially with the labs, for the first time in my career, you can take capital and throw it at a company, and it compounds their advantage."

"How do you screw up a startup? Throw too much money at it and have them hire 1,000 people, and then you create all these coordination issues and overhead issues and dueling priorities... because you can't hire enough people to do enough things fast enough."

"Now that's not the case. You can throw dollars at compute, and compute can make products and the businesses better. So to me, it's not terribly surprising that the power law is more extreme. Right now, economies of scale are a very real thing in the AI market, and I think it'll continue to be the case."

@DavidGeorge83

China is attempting to refill its oil reserves.

Chinese crude imports rose +2.2 million tons in August, to 37.9 million tons, marking their 2nd consecutive monthly increase.

This brings the 2-month increase to ~9.0 million tons, or a ~33% recovery from the total drop between January and July this year.

The increase in crude supply has also allowed China to ramp up fuel exports, with overseas sales of gasoline and diesel surging +29% last month.

However, China's crude imports were down -23% year-over-year and -32% below this year's peak.

Meanwhile, China’s massive oil inventories are estimated at more than 1.2 billion barrels, giving the country ample flexibility to reduce purchases as prices rise.

China's massive oil stockpile is growing again.

The US debt crisis is entering uncharted territory:

Net interest, social security, medicare, healthcare spending, and veterans' benefits currently consume 98.4% of total federal government receipts, near the highest proportion on record.

This figure has surged +28 percentage points since 2022 and is only below the 2020 pandemic peak of ~99.0%.

Net interest alone has nearly tripled as a % of revenue, to a record 19.7%, accounting for roughly half of that +28 percentage-point increase.

By comparison, during the 2008 Financial Crisis, these expenditures did not exceed 90% of federal receipts.

In other words, mandatory spending and interest costs now consume nearly every Dollar the federal government collects.

What is the long-term plan here?

Something broke in the French bond market. Safe bank bonds now yield less than the French government.

The spread just hit a record low. 10-year French covered bonds, the collateralized debt banks issue against pools of mortgages, now yield less than 10-year French government bonds. The market prices a segregated pool of home loans as safer than the French state.

The reason is fiscal. France is running debt at 117% of GDP with a record €310 billion of new bond sales planned for 2026, and its 10-year spread over Germany just hit 90 basis points, the widest since 2012.

When a government's own bonds trade cheaper than the banks it backstops, the balance sheet is the risk. Bond markets discipline governments long before voters do.

The average 30-year mortgage is back near 6.6%, and the Fed cannot wave it down.

Mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury, not the Fed funds rate. That is why they ripped from 2.8% in 2022 to almost 8%, then got stuck in the 6s no matter what the Fed did.

The one lever you actually control is the lender's margin. Your rate has a profit cushion baked in. Get a written quote from a second lender and take it back to your first, and ask them to match or beat it. In the Journal's example, a 6.625% quote used against a 6.875% one.

A quarter point on a $400,000 loan is about $66 a month and roughly $24,000 over the life of the loan. No rate cut from Washington required.

The resale market is a lie detector for luxury.

A Rolex holds about 100% of its sticker price on resale. Wear it for years, sell it for roughly what you paid. A Hermès watch keeps 41%, down from 51% four years ago. Louis Vuitton keeps 35%.

Here is the tell. The Journal reports that many buyers get Hermès watches to build spending history and improve their odds of being allowed to buy a Birkin bag, then resell the watch. That is why it can lose almost 60% the moment it leaves the store.

Resale value is the market pricing real demand. Rolex is a store of value. Most luxury is depreciating consumption wearing an investment costume.

SB Energy has no data centers running and lost $3.2 billion in the first half of 2026. Its pitch is one chart: expected revenue where almost nothing lands in the next two years, and the biggest bar, hundreds of billions of dollars, sits 8 or more years out.

To build it, the company needs over $170 billion of capital. Its anchor customer is OpenAI, which SB Energy lists in its own filing as a risk to that revenue.

This is the AI trade in one picture. Pay for the hype today. Collect the cash next decade, if it shows up.

The market spent three months pricing in Big Pharma's next statin. One trial readout erased it in days.

Amgen ran up 24% this summer on cardiovascular optimism, then gave almost all of it back and sits near +6%. Novartis went from up 6% to down 9%. Novo Nordisk flipped negative too.

The trigger: Novartis's Lp(a) drug pelacarsen cut a genetic driver of heart disease by about 80% and still failed to prevent a single extra heart attack, stroke, or death in its Phase 3 trial.

Lowering the number is not the same as saving a life. Lp(a) was supposed to be Big Pharma's next multibillion-dollar heart franchise. This is binary trial risk in one chart: a single readout can vaporize months of gains across an entire sector.

A struggling sneaker company renamed itself NewBird AI in April. The stock ripped 580% and spiked past $16.

Nothing about the business changed. Same shoes, same losses, new nameplate.

In June it rebranded again to Smartbird and popped another 40%. Today it trades near $2, down about 85% from the April spike.

Slapping AI on the sign is a sell signal, not a strategy. Rebrands that chase a trend trail their peers, and the entire gap comes from companies already losing money. When the name changes to match the headlines, retail becomes the exit liquidity.

$BIRD

Apollo's Torsten Slok says we just went through a regime change, and I agree. For 20 years a savings glut, more capital than projects, crushed interest rates. That era is over.

Now it's a savings shortage. Data centers, the power grid, and above all government deficits are all long-duration claims on a limited pool of savings. Capital finally gets to demand a higher return, and it does so at the long end of the curve.

That is why long rates are rising faster than short. The cheap-money regime that inflated every long-duration asset for two decades is structurally broken, and Washington's borrowing is first in line for the capital.
